title: First Response: Infra Probe & Hot-Swap Plan (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a concise first-response runbook for infra failures that require fast triage and a physical or orchestration-level GPU hot-swap, node cordon/drain, or rapid capacity injection. It prioritizes keeping inference lanes live (fallbacks) and minimizing token-cost/regression risk while we repair hardware or add capacity.

Scope:
- Applies to on-prem and colo racks used for Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Covers: node-level hardware GPU failures, emergency cordon/drain for noisy neighbors, fast capacity backfill, and cluster recovery after partial network/IO failures.
- Not intended for full datacenter evacuation (separate DR runbook).

Quick glossary / assumptions:
- hot-swap: replacing a failed GPU accelerator card or cartridge without lengthy re-provisioning.
- bridge node: temporary worker used to soak traffic while original node is out.
- KV cache priming: warming model caches post-replacement to avoid long-TTFB spikes.

On-call first 10 minutes (rapid probe):
1) Acknowledge alert and set Slack incident channel: #sre-infra-<INC_ID>. PagerDuty -> ENG-SRE escalation policy.
2) Identify impacted pool(s) via Console: check per-route latency and error spike (Console link in linked_artifacts).
3) Run quick health queries (prefer terminal on-call pod or bastion):
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels | grep -E "gpu|dedicated"
   - kubectl top nodes | sort -nr -k3
   - kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,REASON:.status.reason | head
4) Check node-level telemetry: power/temperature/fan errors (monitoring dashboard) and recent kernel oops.
5) If a single node shows hardware fault and is impacting requests, follow cordon/drain flow. If multiple nodes/zone failing -> trigger multi-cluster failover (see escalation).

Node cordon & application-safe drain (recommended default when GPU faulty but removable):
- Goal: move workloads off node with minimal dropped requests and preserve cache where possible.
- Steps:
  1) Mark the node unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node-name>  # prevents new pods
  2) Annotate node with incident id and cause: kubectl annotate node <node-name> sre/incident=<INC_ID> sre/failure=gpu-fault --overwrite
  3) Evict pods gracefully from inference pools: kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='app in (redwood-inference,kv-cache)' --grace-period=45 --timeout=10m
     - If eviction hangs due to long-lived connections, use --force as last resort after notifying product oncall.
  4) Verify pods land on healthy nodes and warm caches: watch kubectl get pods -n redwood-inference -o wide | grep <model-route>
  5) If pods fail to schedule due to quota, trigger capacity add (see section).

Safe physical GPU replacement (for colo racks where hot-swap is possible):
- Prerequisites: follow datacenter safety, grounding strap, and vendor-specific hot-swap guidance. Coordinate with infra techs and SRE lead.
- Steps (high-level):
  1) Confirm node is drained and cordoned. Power-state snapshot: take an AMI/snapshot of any ephemeral logs you need.
  2) Soft-power the node down via BMC: ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U admin -P <redacted> chassis power soft
  3) Physically extract failed accelerator (label with incident id).
  4) Replace with known-good accelerator from staging or hot-spare. Verify part number and firmware.
  5) Power on node via BMC, watch system console for PCIe/driver enumeration.
  6) Post-boot checks:
     - dmesg | tail -n 120  # check for PCIe/driver errors
     - lsmod | grep nvidia (or relevant driver)
     - nvidia-smi -q  # verify card visible, health=OK, ECC errors cleared
  7) Apply vendor firmware/driver if required (documented in linked_artifacts).
  8) Run short smoke inference test on node-local test harness (100 short requests across common routes).
  9) Re-enable scheduling: kubectl uncordon <node-name> and monitor pod placement.

If hot-swap not possible (longer repair):
- Trigger capacity add or spillover to dedicated cloud pool (see Capacity add).
- Ensure fallback routing is enabled for impacted routes (disable region affinity temporarily).

Capacity add (fast backfill)
- Options, in order of preference:
  1) Warm spare nodes (pre-provisioned in colo): promote bridge nodes by flipping labels to dedicated pool.
  2) Cross-cluster spill (route traffic to sibling cluster/region via Console routing policies).
  3) If on-prem burst to cloud is allowed for tenant, trigger auto-scaling job (runbooks/cloud-burst-job).
- Quick steps to add warm spare: 
  - Identify spare node name(s) from inventory: kubectl get nodes -l role=warm-spare -o name
  - Update labels to allow scheduling for the pool: kubectl label node <spare-node> pool=dedicated --overwrite
  - Remove taint that prevented scheduling: kubectl taint nodes <spare-node> node-role.kubernetes.io/spare:NoSchedule-
  - Confirm resource availability and then move traffic (Console routing or config toggle).
- After capacity add: run KV cache priming script against new nodes (scripts/prime-kv.sh <node-list>) to reduce early cold-cache latency.

Cluster recovery after partial network/IO outage:
1) Identify scope (rack, PDU, TOR, SAN). If storage degraded, do NOT power-cycle quickly; consult infra ops.
2) If control-plane degraded (API server flapping), move to secondary control-plane and pause non-essential rollout jobs.
3) For worker nodes showing networking errors, cordon them and follow recovery test: ping to default gateway, check MTU mismatches (ip link, ethtool), check NIC firmware.
4) If cross-zone traffic is impacted, engage network team and enable cross-cluster routing until resolved.

Verification tests (post-fix):
- infra-level: smartctl, nvme-cli, ipmitool SEL checks, dmesg scan for repeated errors.
- infra-service: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,driver_version --format=csv
- perf smoke: run load-script (bench/infer-smoke --qps 50 --duration 120s) against restored nodes and compare P50/P99 to baseline.
- SLO check: ensure % of requests served within latency SLO is back to 99th percentile target for 30m window.

Rollback & fallback considerations:
- If new hardware/driver causes regressions, roll back driver/firmware immediately and mark node restricted for later root-cause.
- If replacing node does not resolve, mark hardware for replacement and move workloads to bridge nodes; open ticket with vendor and procurement.

Logs & artifacts to collect (attach to incident ticket):
- BMC console logs, dmesg, journalctl -u kubelet -n 500, nvidia-smi --query -x output, Prometheus error spikes, pod logs for crashing containers.

Post-incident items (owner: incident lead)
- Run a 1-hour postmortem triage within 48h and a full RCA if customer-impacting.
- Update hardware inventory: mark replaced part, serials, warranty claim.
- Add mitigation in Console: auto-failover thresholds, increase spare pool for that cluster if needed.

Notes to self / open questions (work-in-progress):
- Need a safe no-cache eviction path for long-running KV caches that still lets us move traffic without huge cold-start penalty.
- Investigate automating warm-spare promotion when node health < 70% for 5m.
- Audit whether burst-to-cloud is allowed for all tenants; add guardrails in Console.

Quick checklist (copy into incident channel):
- [ ] Create incident channel and tag on-call
- [ ] Identify impacted model routes and pools
- [ ] Cordon and drain node(s) if single-node fault
- [ ] Promote warm spare or add capacity if needed
- [ ] Perform physical replacement or schedule vendor RMA
- [ ] Run post-fix smoke tests and SLO verification
- [ ] Collect logs and attach to ticket
- [ ] Schedule postmortem and update runbook after findings

End of draft. Please add hardware-specific vendor steps under 'linked_artifacts' and flag anything risky in the incident channel.
